To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
overshoot is best predicted by a model of auditory nerve activity that includes the effects of MCO efferent feedback.
the effects of MCO efferent feedback are necessary to explain overshoot and that cochlear hearing loss reduces the magnitude of overshoot only in simulations that include MCO effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of cochlear hearing loss on auditory processing.
the role of the medial olivococlear (MOC), a system of auditory neurons that project from the superior olivary complex to the cochlea, in hearing loss and hearing protection.
the role of efferent feedback in the auditory system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MOC efferents are necessary to explain overshoot, but not sufficient to explain overshoot.
the overshoot phenomenon is a consequence of the dynamic range adaptation of auditory nerve fibers.
overshoot in both normal and hearing-imparied listeners can only be accounted for when both MOC efferents and dynamic range adaptation are included in the model.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MOC reflex is a key factor for overshoot and that cochlear hearing loss reduces its contribution.
the overshoot phenomenon can be explained as a dynamic-range-adaptation mechanism that operates in parallel with MOC efferents.
the overshoot phenomenon is mediated by the medial olivococlear efferent feedback system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MOC efferents are a promising candidate to explain overshoot in normal hearing, as well as the reduced overshoot observed in cochlear hearing loss.
the MOC reflex can explain a variety of perceptual phenomena that are not well accounted for by the firing rate adaptation observed in anesthetized animal preparations.
the overshoot in masked tone-pip detection is a robust phenomenon in normal and hearing impaired listeners, but the mechanism of this overshoot may be different in these populations.
